title: Protein folding (HP model)
tagline: Fold a chain of amino acids on a grid so its water-fearing parts huddle together.
statement: Each case is a protein chain written with two letters: H (hydrophobic, it avoids water) and P (polar). Fold it on a square grid: each amino acid sits on its own cell, and consecutive ones are neighbours. Every pair of H that touch on the grid without being consecutive in the chain counts -1. Lowest energy wins. This 2D HP model is a classic benchmark of protein folding research: proven optimal folds are known up to 80 amino acids; for 85 and 100, the best known energies may still be beaten.
format: { "moves": "RRULLDR..." }  (n-1 letters, absolute directions: R right, L left, U up, D down; the chain starts at (0,0))

world_source.label: Standard 2D HP benchmarks (Unger & Moult 1993; Istrail benchmark), best known energies as compiled in BMC Bioinformatics 6:30 (2005)

strategies: Monte Carlo with pull moves (local moves that keep the chain self-avoiding), at a slowly decreasing temperature.
Build the fold residue by residue with a growth method (PERM style): keep the most promising partial chains, prune the rest.
Aim for a compact hydrophobic core first: place H residues in a dense block, then route the P residues around it.
Start from the current best fold and apply crankshaft and end moves to free trapped H pairs.
Replica exchange: run several temperatures in parallel and swap configurations.
Constraint search: treat it as a self-avoiding walk problem and use branch and bound on the number of H-H contacts still possible.
